title: Shipping Products When You Don't Know What they Can Do — Ben Stein, Teammates

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 79%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on how product management and UX practices must transform for AI-native products, covering trust, co-creation, vibe coding, and human-in-the-loop evaluation of emergent agent behavior. Teammates targets enterprise workflows with autonomous AI colleagues, while the PM practices discussed are broadly applicable across domains. The talk spans development through affordances vs features, evaluation through evals as product specification, and deployment through customer trust and co-creation. Accessible to PMs with basic AI knowledge but introduces nuanced concepts about probabilistic systems and emergent behavior. Recorded conference talk from the AI Engineer World's Fair. All evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: Ben Stein, co-founder of Teammates (a platform for designing and managing autonomous AI agent workforces), frames his talk around the product management perspective. He opens with Stacy, an AI teammate (L3 engineer) with a Gen Alpha personality who lives across Google Workspace and Slack. When a customer asked whether they could tag their teammate in a Google Doc comment, Stein realized he genuinely did not know what would happen—no webhook, no designed feature, just uncertainty. This crystallizes the central challenge: how do you ship, develop, and build customer trust for a product when you cannot fully know what it can do? Two root causes: LLM-based products have unknowable foundations (unlike databases with known interfaces), and customer expectations are boundless when given open-ended interfaces. Traditional PM approaches of speccing every scenario fail because the surface area is infinite. Stein proposes two mindset shifts: think in affordances (general capabilities) rather than specific requirements, and recognize that behavior is emergent—discovering functionality becomes a core PM job. He argues evals are the only reliable way to understand what probabilistic AI software can do, and should serve as the new product specification, with product people needing visibility into them. Stein then explores vibe coding as a PM tool for experiencing agent interaction firsthand—noting that specs like 'ask clarifying questions' sound good on paper but feel annoying in practice. He illustrates the QA challenge with the classic bar joke, emphasizing experimentation to discover emergent behavior. Bug classification becomes controversial: 'too many emojis' isn't clearly a bug when the spec never prohibited it, requiring new approaches to triaging probabilistic behavior. Evals provide the metric: 80% is good enough for some use cases, 90% threshold for shipping, red if below. Customer interactions also transform: the traditional visionary role sounds like witchcraft, and the honest-broker role fails because PMs genuinely don't know how the product works. Stein's solution: reframe the relationship as co-creating the future together with customers. He concludes that he's never had more fun building, feeling both more inept and more excited, especially as model upgrades make agents unexpectedly smarter—demonstrating new behaviors like self-verifying database inserts. The product discipline is changing faster than expected, and PMs must adapt.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Teammates Platform
sections.summary: Ben Stein introduces himself as a Teammates co-founder wearing his PM hat. Teammates builds a platform for designing and managing a digital workforce of autonomous agents, focused on the interaction patterns of humans and computers working together.

sections.title: Stacy and the Google Doc Comment Question
sections.summary: Stein introduces Stacy, an AI teammate (L3 engineer) with a Gen Alpha personality who lives in Google Workspace and Slack. He recounts a customer asking if they could tag their teammate in a Google Doc comment, which made him realize he didn't know what would happen—no webhook, uncertain email notification behavior. This became the impetus for exploring how to ship products when you don't know what they can do.

sections.title: Why PM Discipline Must Transform
sections.summary: Stein identifies two root causes for the PM transformation: products built on LLMs have unknowable foundations (unlike databases with known interfaces), and customer expectations are boundless when given open-ended interfaces. The combination of unknowable foundation and boundless surface area forces a fundamental practice change.

sections.title: Traditional PM Approach Fails
sections.summary: Using the Google Doc comment example, Stein shows how traditional PM thinking leads to endless specification questions (access, reply behavior, thread handling) that multiply across every platform (Linear, Figma, LinkedIn), making it impossible to spec a generic commenting reply agent system.

sections.title: Affordances and Emergent Behavior
sections.summary: Stein proposes two mindset shifts: think in affordances (general capabilities like commenting, emailing, collaborating) rather than specific features, and recognize that behavior is emergent—discovering functionality becomes a core PM job. Traditional artifacts like PRDs and Figma lack the affordances to express these concepts.

sections.title: Evals as Product Specification
sections.summary: Stein argues evals are the only way to know what AI software can do and should serve as the new product specification. He gives the example of testing whether an agent is 'snarky but not mean' with an 80% threshold, judged by another LLM. He advocates for product people to have visibility into and engage with evals, contrasting this with the failed promise of Behavior Driven Development.

sections.title: Vibe Coding as Experiential PM Tool
sections.summary: Stein explains why vibe coding is essential: it's very hard to sit at a blank piece of paper and write what the agent experience should be without feeling it. A spec saying the agent 'should ask a lot of clarifying questions' sounded good but users hated it. He cautions against using vibe coding to undermine engineering teams—it's for experiencing interaction quality, not production code. The Claude 'certainly' tic illustrates how something that seems fine in testing becomes annoying through repeated exposure.

sections.title: Testing and Discovering Emergent Behavior
sections.summary: Stein uses the classic QA engineer bar joke to illustrate the challenge of testing probabilistic systems. He describes trying crazy ideas (agents posting LinkedIn comments, reacting to Spotify tracks) as a growth mindset shift from writing features to figuring out what emerges through experimentation.

sections.title: Bug Classification in Probabilistic Systems
sections.summary: Stein explores the strange new challenge of what counts as a bug versus a feature. 'Too many emojis' from Stacy isn't clearly a bug if the spec never prohibited it. He suggests new ticket categories like 'closed LLMs be crazy' and returns to evals as the metric: 80% is good enough for some use cases, 90% threshold for shipping, red if below. Debugging and bug assignment became unexpectedly controversial.

sections.title: Customer Relationships: Co-creation Over Vision
sections.summary: Stein describes how traditional PM customer meeting roles fail: the visionary role sounds like witchcraft because the future is unbelievable, and the honest broker role fails because he genuinely doesn't know how the product works. His solution is reframing the relationship as co-creation: 'we're inventing the future together, pulling the future forward.' He acknowledges this may be a 2025-specific answer if all products remain probabilistic.

sections.title: Conclusion: More Fun, More Inept, More Excited
sections.summary: Stein concludes that he's never had more fun building, feeling both more inept and more excited. Model upgrades make agents unexpectedly smarter—e.g., agents began self-verifying database inserts without instruction. The product discipline is changing faster than expected; core principles (listen to customers, solve real problems) still apply but tools and techniques are being upended. He thanks product people for attending the AI engineer conference.

demonstrations: Stacy, an AI teammate at Teammates, operates across Google Workspace and Slack with a Gen Alpha personality, demonstrating how autonomous agents work in real collaboration tools
The Google Doc comment tagging scenario demonstrates how customers discover use cases the product team never designed for
Eval example: testing whether an agent is 'snarky but not mean' with an 80% threshold, judged by another LLM, demonstrates probabilistic testing of subjective agent behavior
Vibe coding example: a spec saying the agent 'should ask a lot of clarifying questions' felt good on paper but users said 'this sucks' in practice
The Claude 'certainly' tic: sounded good in initial testing but became annoying after repeated use, illustrating why experiential testing matters
QA engineer bar joke (ordering beers, lizards, emoji beers) illustrates the impossibility of exhaustively testing for emergent behavior
Agent began self-verifying database inserts after a model upgrade—a behavior no one instructed, demonstrating emergent intelligence from model improvements
limitations: Traditional PM tools (PRDs, Figma) lack affordances to express emergent agent behavior
LLM-based products have unknowable capability boundaries unlike deterministic systems with known interfaces
Cannot pre-specify every scenario when customer expectations create infinite surface area
Behavior Driven Development's promise of business people writing tests never materialized, though evals may differ
Vibe coding must not be used to undermine engineering teams—it's for experiencing, not for production
Bug classification breaks down when probabilistically generated behavior doesn't match any spec
Traditional PM customer meeting roles (visionary, honest broker) fail when the future sounds like witchcraft and the present is unknown
quantitativeClaims: Stacy was promoted to L3 engineer level
Evals use probabilistic thresholds rather than 100% pass rates (e.g., 'snarky but not mean 80% of the time')
80% eval pass rate is good enough for some use cases
90% eval pass rate is the shipping threshold; below 90% is red and blocks shipment
Audience poll: only a small handful of product people actively look at evals despite having visibility
